nationality_or_literary_tradition: Nigerian; Igbo novelist, short-story writer and children's author, born and raised in Northern Nigeria, who chaired Biafra's Bureau for External Publicity during the civil war
literary_identity: Nigerian novelist and pioneer of the popular urban novel, whose People of the City (1954) was among the first West African novels in English and whose Jagua Nana (1961) became the best-known Nigerian popular novel; also a prolific writer of folk tales, novellas and books for young readers from 1947 to the 1990s.
biography: Cyprian Odiatu Duaka Ekwensi was born on 26 September 1921 at Minna in Northern Nigeria, to Igbo parents from Nkwelle Ezunaka, in present-day Anambra State (Wikipedia). Contemporary Black Biography says that he grew up speaking Hausa as well as Igbo, and that his father, David Duaka, a storyteller and elephant hunter, told him the Igbo tales he later published. He was educated at Government College, Ibadan, at Achimota College in the Gold Coast and at the School of Forestry, worked for two years as a forestry officer, and taught biology, chemistry and English at Igbobi College, Lagos, from 1947 to 1949, the years of his first books. Trained as a pharmacist, he lectured at the School of Pharmacy in Lagos (1949-1956), and in 1951 a government scholarship took him to the Chelsea School of Pharmacy in London; he wrote People of the City on the voyage. Gale dates his first work for the Nigerian Broadcasting Corporation to 1951; Contemporary Authors makes him head of features there from 1957 to 1961, when he became federal director of information. He read his stories on the radio, where he was known as 'Your Favourite Story Teller'. In 1966 he resigned and moved his family to Enugu; during the civil war he chaired Biafra's Bureau for External Publicity and directed its radio service, and travelled to the United States to raise money for Biafra. After the war he ran newspaper and publishing companies in the East (managing director of the Daily Star, 1975-1979), chaired the East Central State Library Board (1972-1975) and, according to Gale, the Federal Radio Corporation of Nigeria from 1991; Contemporary Black Biography says he wrote full time from 1984. He received the Dag Hammarskjold International Prize for Literary Merit (1969 in Gale's entries, 1968 in Wikipedia), was made a Member of the Order of the Federal Republic in 2001 and a fellow of the Nigerian Academy of Letters in 2006, and died at Enugu on 4 November 2007. He married Eunice Anyiwo; they had five children.
literary_profile: Ekwensi's books of the period run from When Love Whispers and Ikolo the Wrestler (both 1947) to King Forever! and Masquerade Time (1992) and The Red Flag (1993). His adult novels are People of the City (1954), Jagua Nana (1961), Burning Grass (1962), Beautiful Feathers (1963), Iska (1966), Survive the Peace (1976), Divided We Stand (1980), and Jagua Nana's Daughter and For a Roll of Parchment (both 1986 or 1987). His collections of stories include The Rainmaker (1965), Lokotown (1966) and Restless City and Christmas Gold (1975), and Contemporary Authors lists twenty-one juvenile titles, among them The Leopard's Claw (1950), The Drummer Boy and The Passport of Mallam Ilia (1960) and An African Night's Entertainment (1962). He also wrote hundreds of stories for newspapers, magazines and radio, and radio and television scripts for the BBC and Radio Nigeria. Emmanuel Iduma puts his output at nearly forty novels by his death; Cosentino notes that the U.S. edition of Jagua Nana (1969) already listed seven novellas, four works of folklore, two collections of stories and six novels.
stylistic_characteristics: Ekwensi called himself 'a writer for the masses', more interested in 'the heart of the truth which the man in the street can recognize' than in style (interview with Lewis Nkosi, 1972, quoted in Contemporary Black Biography). His novels are episodic, a habit the Encyclopedia of World Biography traces to his beginnings as a pamphleteer and Contemporary Black Biography to the radio stories out of which People of the City grew. Juliet Okonkwo compares his naturalistic technique with Zola's; John Povey sees behind it a reading of American popular fiction and crime paperbacks. Dialogue moves between Pidgin, broken English and standard Nigerian English, sometimes within one paragraph, and his descriptions of dress borrow the language of advertising in Drum magazine (Cosentino).
intellectual_concerns: The modern West African city, above all Lagos, as a place of opportunity, corruption and moral danger for migrants from the countryside; women's independence and its price (Jagua Nana, Iska, Jagua Nana's Daughter); party politics and corruption at the end of colonial rule and after independence; Pan-African solidarity set against domestic failure (Beautiful Feathers); ethnic hostility, civil war and the hardships of the peace (Iska, Survive the Peace, Divided We Stand); colour prejudice met by African students in England (For a Roll of Parchment); and, in the folk tales and children's books, vengeance, heroism, adventure and moral instruction.
historical_significance: Gale's Contextual Encyclopedia calls him the father of the modern Nigerian novel, and Martin Tucker the earliest and most prolific of the socially realistic Nigerian novelists (quoted in Contemporary Authors). People of the City preceded Achebe's Things Fall Apart by four years, and Charles Larson thought him probably the most widely read novelist in Nigeria. His standing with critics has been lower: Bernth Lindfors found none of his works free of 'amateurish blots and blunders', while his biographer Ernest Emenyonu saw in them 'a literature of social awareness and commitment'. He links the Onitsha market pamphlets, where he began, with the novel published in London, and the St. James Guide to Children's Writers calls him an acknowledged pioneer of Nigerian writing for young readers.

After 2000: Cash on Delivery (stories, 2007, according to Wikipedia). Dates that differ between sources are given in the work records.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Indian; novelist, short-story writer and essayist writing in English, from a Tamil family of Madras, who lived in Mysore and set almost all his fiction in the imaginary South Indian town of Malgudi
literary_identity: Indian novelist and short-story writer, with Mulk Raj Anand and Raja Rao a leading author of early Indian writing in English (Wikipedia); his fourteen novels, from Swami and Friends (1935) to The World of Nagaraj (1990), are almost all set in Malgudi, as are most of his stories, and The Guide (1958) won the first Sahitya Akademi Award for a book in English.
biography: Rasipuram Krishnaswami Narayanaswami was born in Madras on 10 October 1906 into a Tamil Brahmin family and spent part of his childhood in the care of his maternal grandmother, Parvati, while his father, a headmaster, was transferred from school to school (Wikipedia). In 1922 he joined the school in Mysore where his father was headmaster; he failed the entrance examination twice and took his BA at Maharaja's College, Mysore, in 1930 (Gale's Contextual Encyclopedia; Contemporary Authors). A brief spell as a schoolteacher proved distasteful, and he turned to writing: an article on Indian cinema in the Madras Mail (July 1930) was his first publication, and he later reported from Mysore for the newspaper Justice. Graham Greene, shown the manuscript by a friend, recommended Swami and Friends, which Hamish Hamilton published in 1935; Contemporary Authors says he shortened his surname to Narayan that year. He married Rajam in 1934; they had a daughter, Hema, and Rajam's death in 1939 stopped his writing for a time. He edited the journal Indian Thought from 1941 and owned Indian Thought Publications in Mysore, which issued many of his books in India. After The English Teacher (1945) came the novels of the period studied here, from Mr. Sampath (1949) to The World of Nagaraj (1990), together with stories, essays, travel writing, a memoir and prose versions of the Ramayana and the Mahabharata; My Dateless Diary records his first visit to the United States, in 1956. His honours include the Sahitya Akademi Award for The Guide (1960; Contemporary Authors gives 1961), the Padma Bhushan (1964), the English-Speaking Union Book Award for My Days (1975), the Royal Society of Literature's Benson Medal (1980), honorary membership of the American Academy and Institute of Arts and Letters (1981 in Wikipedia, 1982 in Contemporary Authors), the Sahitya Akademi Fellowship (1994) and the Padma Vibhushan (2000). He sat in the Rajya Sabha as a nominated member from 1986 to 1992. His brother R. K. Laxman, the cartoonist, illustrated some of his books. He died in Chennai on 13 May 2001; his manuscripts are in the Mugar Memorial Library at Boston University.
literary_profile: Narayan's books of 1946-2000 comprise ten novels, from Mr. Sampath (1949) to The World of Nagaraj (1990); story collections from An Astrologer's Day and Other Stories (1947) and Lawley Road (1956) to Malgudi Days (1982), Under the Banyan Tree (1985), The Grandmother's Tale (1992) and Salt and Sawdust (1993); retellings of Indian myth in Gods, Demons, and Others (1964) and shortened prose versions of the Ramayana (1972) and the Mahabharata (1978); travel writing (My Dateless Diary, 1960; The Emerald Route, 1977, which includes the play The Watchman of the Lake); essays (Next Sunday, 1956; Reluctant Guru, 1974; A Writer's Nightmare, 1988); and the memoir My Days (1974). He also wrote stories for magazines, among them the New Yorker (Contemporary Authors) and Playboy, which printed 'A Breath of Lucifer' in July 1969 and 'God and the Cobbler' in February 1976 (Post45 Playboy Fiction Index).
stylistic_characteristics: Narayan told William Walsh that English 'is so transparent it can take on the tint of any country', and Walsh called his English 'limpid, simple, calm and unaffected, natural in its run and tone, and beautifully measured' (Contemporary Authors). Walsh also described the typical design of the novels as concentric circles, with the town outside, the family within and a modest, self-aware hero at the hub, and called them 'comedies of sadness'. Melvin J. Friedman placed him, with Isaac Bashevis Singer, in an oral tradition in which the spoken triumphs over the written. Gale's Contextual Encyclopedia stresses the economy of his plotting, and notes that the stories of his early collections are slight and journalistic, those of the later ones longer and more intricately built.
intellectual_concerns: Middle-class life in a small South Indian town and the meeting of tradition and modernity there; money, ambition and the vanity of human wishes (The Financial Expert); imposture and sainthood (The Guide); the national movement and Gandhi (Waiting for the Mahatma); fathers and sons and the generation gap (The Vendor of Sweets); a bully's invasion of a quiet life, told through a Hindu myth (The Man-Eater of Malgudi); love set against a woman's vocation (The Painter of Signs); renunciation and detachment (A Tiger for Malgudi); the retelling of Hindu myth and epic; and the comedy of misunderstanding between India and the West ('A Horse and Two Goats', Talkative Man).
historical_significance: Graham Greene called him 'the novelist I most admire in the English language' (Contemporary Authors), the poet Dom Moraes 'by far the best writer of English fiction that his country has ever produced' (Gale), and Shashi Tharoor wrote that in the West he was widely considered the quintessential Indian writer. Critics compare Malgudi with Faulkner's Yoknapatawpha County, and Walsh wrote that 'whatever happens in India happens in Malgudi, and whatever happens in Malgudi happens everywhere'. The Guide won the first Sahitya Akademi Award for English, and in 1994 he became the second Indian writer in English, after Anand, to be made a Fellow of the Akademi. V. S. Naipaul's reading of his novels as 'religious books ... intensely Hindu', prepared for withdrawal rather than action, is a political critique that later critics, Richard Cronin among them, have examined (eNotes).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; Indiana novelist, author of a single published book, Raintree County (1948)
literary_identity: American novelist whose only published book, Raintree County (1948), an epic of nineteenth-century Indiana framed by a single day, 4 July 1892, was a bestseller and has been named as a candidate for the Great American Novel; he took his own life two months after it appeared.
biography: Ross Franklin Lockridge Jr. was born on 25 April 1914 in Bloomington, Indiana, the youngest of four children of Elsie Shockley and Ross Lockridge Sr., a populist historian and lecturer; the novelist Mary Jane Ward was his double cousin (Wikipedia). He graduated from Indiana University in 1935 with the highest average then recorded there, after a year at the Sorbonne, taught English at the university while writing an MA thesis on Byron and Napoleon, and married Vernice Baker in 1936. In 1940 he went to Harvard on a fellowship and later taught at Simmons College in Boston; a long poem, The Dream of the Flesh of Iron, was rejected by Houghton Mifflin in 1941. From the summer of 1943 he typed Raintree County on the backs of the pages of a 2,000-page draft about his mother's family, and finished it as a 600,000-word typescript in April 1946. Houghton Mifflin accepted it, and an MGM prize of $150,000 and a Book-of-the-Month Club selection followed, each at the price of further cuts. The novel was published on 5 January 1948 to extravagant reviews and large sales. Suffering from severe depression, Lockridge died of carbon monoxide poisoning in Bloomington on 6 March 1948, leaving his wife and four young children. John Leggett paired his life with Thomas Heggen's in Ross and Tom: Two American Tragedies (1974), and his son Larry Lockridge wrote the biography Shade of the Raintree (1994).
literary_profile: His published work is Raintree County (Houghton Mifflin, 1948). Earlier writing, a long poem rejected in 1941 and a family novel with the working title American Lives, was not published (Wikipedia).
stylistic_characteristics: Raintree County mixes realist chronicle with dream sequences, flashbacks and departures from linear narrative, and confines its present action to one day, perhaps in emulation of Joyce's Ulysses, as Wikipedia suggests; Howard Mumford Jones found in it 'a queer amalgam of pattern and formlessness'.
intellectual_concerns: The American myth and the meaning of the Civil War; the Midwest as the heart of the republic; heroism, poetry and the quest for an ideal, figured in the legendary golden raintree; a marriage across the sectional divide.
historical_significance: Raintree County was a New York Times bestseller (Post45) that the Times reviewer called 'a huge and extraordinary first novel', while the New Yorker dismissed it as 'the climax of all the swollen, pretentious human chronicles'; MGM filmed it in 1957. Lockridge's suicide at the height of its success made him, with Heggen, the subject of Leggett's study of two first novelists destroyed by sudden fame.
bibliographical_notes: Bibliography status, 1946-2000: complete for published books. Lockridge published one book, Raintree County (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1948; recorded). An excerpt appeared in Life on 18 September 1947. Unpublished: The Dream of the Flesh of Iron (a long poem rejected by Houghton Mifflin in 1941), the abandoned family novel American Lives, on whose typescript the novel was drafted, and his MA thesis on Byron and Napoleon (Indiana University). Sources: Wikipedia's articles on Lockridge and the novel, and the Post45 New York Times bestseller data.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; novelist and playwright, born in Iowa, whose family moved to Oklahoma City in 1935; author of Mister Roberts (1946)
literary_identity: American novelist whose only book, Mister Roberts (1946), a novel of life aboard a US Navy cargo ship in the rear areas of the Pacific war, sold over a million copies; with Joshua Logan he turned it into the play that won the Tony Awards for best play and best author in 1948.
biography: Thomas Heggen was born on 23 December 1918 in Fort Dodge, Iowa; in 1935, when his father's business failed in the Depression, the family moved to Oklahoma City (Wikipedia). He was a cousin of Wallace Stegner. After Oklahoma City University and Oklahoma State University he took a journalism degree at the University of Minnesota, where Max Shulman was a classmate, and became an editor at Reader's Digest in New York. He joined the Navy after Pearl Harbor, was commissioned a lieutenant in August 1942, and served on supply ships in the North Atlantic, the Caribbean and the Pacific, including fourteen months as assistant communications officer of the cargo ship USS Virgo, where he wrote vignettes of shipboard tedium and clashed with a martinet captain. Discharged in December 1945, he reworked them into Mister Roberts (Houghton Mifflin, 1946), which sold over a million copies despite mixed reviews. A stage adaptation begun with Shulman failed; written instead with the producer-director Joshua Logan, the play opened at the Alvin Theatre on 18 February 1948 with Henry Fonda and ran for 1,157 performances. Under pressure to write another bestseller, Heggen suffered from writer's block and insomnia, which he treated with alcohol and sleeping pills; on 19 May 1949 he drowned in his bath in New York after taking barbiturates. His death was widely reported as a probable suicide, though he left no note and friends insisted it was an accident (Wikipedia).
literary_profile: Mister Roberts (novel; Houghton Mifflin, 1946) and, with Joshua Logan, the play Mister Roberts (first performed in 1948; published by Random House, 1948).
stylistic_characteristics: Episodic chapters grown out of separate shipboard stories, mixing barracks comedy with frustration and a tragic ending; Logan's stage version stressed the farce while keeping the serious undertones (Wikipedia).
intellectual_concerns: The boredom and pettiness of the rear areas of the Pacific war; an officer who shields his men from a tyrannical captain while longing for combat; the crew's loyalty; men who feel 'left out' of the war.
historical_significance: Mister Roberts sold over a million copies and was a New York Times bestseller (Post45); the play made from it with Logan won the first Tony Award for Best Play and was filmed in 1955 with Henry Fonda. John Leggett paired Heggen with Ross Lockridge in Ross and Tom (1974) as two first novelists whose deaths followed sudden success.
bibliographical_notes: Bibliography status, 1946-2000: complete for books. Recorded: Mister Roberts (novel; Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1946). Listed and not recorded here: Mister Roberts, the play written with Joshua Logan (Alvin Theatre, New York, 18 February 1948; New York: Random House, 1948, with a foreword by John Mason Brown), which the Pulitzer drama jury considered for 1948 (Wikipedia's Pulitzer list, via the discovery inventory); it will be recorded when Logan, who has no record yet, is researched, so that both authors are credited. The shipboard stories from which the novel grew were not identified separately in the sources consulted.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; novelist from Massachusetts, of an Irish Catholic family, who lived in Italy from 1950
literary_identity: American novelist, author of three novels: The Gallery (1947), portraits of Allied-occupied Naples in 1944, was a bestseller praised by Hemingway and Edmund Wilson, while Lucifer with a Book (1949) and A Cry of Children (1952) were savaged by reviewers, and his reputation faded until The Gallery was reissued in 2004.
biography: John Horne Burns was born on 7 October 1916 in Andover, Massachusetts, the eldest of seven children of an upper-middle-class Irish Catholic family, and was educated at St Augustine's School, Phillips Academy and Harvard, where he became fluent in French, German and Italian and wrote the book for a student musical comedy (Wikipedia). He graduated in 1937 and taught English at the Loomis School in Windsor, Connecticut, writing several novels that he never published. Drafted in 1942, he was commissioned as a second lieutenant and served in military intelligence in Casablanca and Algiers and then for eighteen months in Italy, mainly in Naples, where he censored prisoners' mail. Back at Loomis after his discharge in 1946, he finished The Gallery, which Harper published in 1947; it became a bestseller. Lucifer with a Book (1949), a satire of a boarding school like Loomis, was savagely reviewed, and in 1950 he moved to Florence, where he wrote A Cry of Children (1952) and an article on the city for Holiday, and began a fourth novel. Known for his drinking and his attacks on other writers, he died of a cerebral haemorrhage after a sailing trip, on 11 August 1953, aged thirty-six, and was buried in Brookline, Massachusetts. David Margolick wrote his biography, Dreadful: The Short Life and Gay Times of John Horne Burns (2013), and called him, in the New York Times Magazine, 'the great (gay) novelist you've never heard of' (Wikipedia).
literary_profile: Three novels, all published by Harper: The Gallery (1947), Lucifer with a Book (1949) and A Cry of Children (1952). He also wrote book reviews for the New York Times and the Saturday Review, a piece on Florence for Holiday and, in Harper's Magazine (May 1947), 'Promenade in Naples'; a fourth novel was unfinished at his death.
stylistic_characteristics: The Gallery alternates nine character portraits with eight first-person recollections by an anonymous American soldier; Paul Fussell said Burns 'relied on discontinuity, like a sort of prose T. S. Eliot' (Wikipedia). Reviewers of the later novels found the same gift for biting satire and drama turned to caricature and excess (Kirkus).
intellectual_concerns: Occupiers and occupied in wartime Naples; the soldier's resentment of the military machine; homosexual servicemen; hypocrisy and venality in American private education; destructive love and a possessive mother; the veteran as smashed idealist.
historical_significance: The Gallery was called 'the best war book of the year' by the Saturday Review and praised by Hemingway, Edmund Wilson and John Dos Passos; by 1991 Herbert Mitgang called it 'that forgotten gem of a novel', and New York Review Books reissued it in 2004 with an introduction by Paul Fussell. Time noted its chapter on 'an evening spent in a homosexuals' hangout', which other reviewers left unmentioned, and later critics, among them Marisa Escolar, have read it for its portrayal of homosexual servicemen (Wikipedia).
bibliographical_notes: Bibliography status, 1946-2000: complete for books; periodical writing incomplete. Recorded: The Gallery (New York: Harper & Brothers, 1947); Lucifer with a Book (Harper, 1949); A Cry of Children (Harper, 1952; Wikipedia's list of works gives 1951, its text and Kirkus 1952). Not recorded: reviews in the New York Times (1949) and the Saturday Review (1948-49); 'Promenade in Naples' (Harper's Magazine, May 1947, seen in the Unz Review's index as a search extract); a piece on Florence for Holiday; the unfinished fourth novel; and the unpublished early novels and student work held at the Howard Gotlieb Archival Research Center, Boston University. The chapter 'Queen Penicillin' from The Gallery was anthologised as a story in The Best Short Stories of World War II (1957) and American Men at Arms (1964).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; African American novelist, short-story writer and journalist of Boston and Martha's Vineyard, associated with the Harlem Renaissance
literary_identity: African American novelist and short-story writer of the Harlem Renaissance generation and founder of the magazine Challenge, whose two novels, The Living Is Easy (1948) and The Wedding (1995), satirise and chronicle the Black middle class of Boston and Martha's Vineyard.
biography: Dorothy West was born in Boston on 2 June 1907, the daughter of Rachel Benson, of Camden, South Carolina, and Isaac Christopher West, a former slave who built a wholesale fruit business and was known as Boston's 'Black Banana King'; the family was among the most affluent Black households in the city, and the poet Helene Johnson was her cousin (Wikipedia). She published her first story at fourteen, attended the Girls' Latin School, Boston University and the Columbia School of Journalism, and in 1926 tied with Zora Neale Hurston for second place in Opportunity's contest with 'The Typewriter'. In Harlem she knew Langston Hughes, Countee Cullen and Wallace Thurman; she took a small part in Porgy and went with it to London in 1929, travelled to the Soviet Union in 1932 with a group making a film about American racism, founded Challenge in 1934 (six issues, to 1937) and edited its successor, New Challenge, with Richard Wright. She worked as a welfare investigator and for the Federal Writers' Project, wrote stories for the New York Daily News, and in the mid-1940s settled in her family's house at Oak Bluffs on Martha's Vineyard, where she wrote The Living Is Easy (Houghton Mifflin, 1948). For four decades she wrote for the island's newspaper. The Feminist Press reissued her novel in 1982, and with the encouragement of Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis, her editor at Doubleday, she finished The Wedding (1995), which Oprah Winfrey adapted for television in 1998; the collection The Richer, the Poorer followed in 1995. She died in Boston on 16 August 1998 (Wikipedia; Kirkus).
literary_profile: Two novels, The Living Is Easy (Houghton Mifflin, 1948) and The Wedding (Doubleday, 1995); short stories from the 1920s onwards in Opportunity, The Crisis, the Saturday Evening Quill and the New York Daily News, many collected with sketches and reminiscences in The Richer, the Poorer (Doubleday, 1995); a weekly column for the Vineyard Gazette from 1948; and the magazines Challenge (1934-37) and New Challenge, which she edited.
stylistic_characteristics: Ironic humour and close social observation: Seymour Krim called The Living Is Easy 'a housewifey novel: a look at life from the kitchen and the parlor', full of 'abundant and special woman's energy' (Wikipedia), and Kirkus found her strength as 'a moralist and social observer', with her best stories told from a young girl's point of view.
intellectual_concerns: Class and colour within Black society, especially among the light-skinned elite Kirkus called the 'blue-white' Black people of Boston; ambition and the American dream; women's power within the family; poverty and welfare in Depression Harlem; childhood.
historical_significance: One of the few Black women writers published in major literary magazines in the 1930s and 1940s and, late in life, celebrated as one of the last surviving members of the Harlem Renaissance (Wikipedia). Cynthia Davis argues that her concentration on the Black middle class placed her 'outside the black vernacular tradition' of Petry, Wright and Baldwin and left her less studied; the Feminist Press reissue of 1982 and the success of The Wedding brought her renewed attention.
bibliographical_notes: Bibliography status, 1946-2000: substantially complete for books; periodical work not listed piece by piece. Recorded: The Living Is Easy (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1948; reissued by the Feminist Press, 1982); The Wedding (New York: Doubleday, 1995); The Richer, the Poorer: Stories, Sketches, and Reminiscences (Doubleday, 1995). Not recorded individually: her stories of the 1940s for the New York Daily News and, Wikipedia says, The New Yorker; her Vineyard Gazette columns from 1948; and her essay of 1985 on Sergei Eisenstein, later collected in The Richer, the Poorer. Before the period, and not recorded by installment 9: her stories from 'Promise and Fulfillment' (Boston Post) and 'The Typewriter' (Opportunity, 1926) onwards, and her editorship of Challenge (1934-37) and New Challenge.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; African American novelist and journalist from Philadelphia, an expatriate in France from 1951
literary_identity: African American novelist and journalist of the postwar protest tradition, author of Last of the Conquerors (1948), South Street (1954) and The Stone Face (1963), one of the earliest fictional accounts of the Paris massacre of 17 October 1961; he lived in France from 1951 and worked for Agence France-Presse.
biography: William Gardner Smith was born in Philadelphia on 6 February 1927 and grew up in the South Philadelphia ghetto, a recurring setting of his novels (Wikipedia, quoting the Dictionary of Literary Biography). With his high-school principal's help he began reporting part-time for the Pittsburgh Courier, graduated with honours in January 1944 and joined the paper full-time. Drafted in January 1946, he served as a clerk-typist in occupied Berlin, the source of his first novel, Last of the Conquerors (1948), published when he was twenty-one. After his discharge he studied at Temple University, married and wrote Anger at Innocence (1950); after a stay at Yaddo the couple left for France in late 1951, joining the African American community in Paris that included Richard Wright, James Baldwin and Chester Himes. The marriage failed. South Street (1954) appeared as he joined Agence France-Presse, for which he worked as an editor and correspondent, directing its service in Ghana until Nkrumah's fall in 1966. The Stone Face (1963) drew on the anti-Arab racism of the Algerian War years in Paris, and Return to Black America (1970) revised reporting from his visits to the United States in the late 1960s, when French radio and television treated him as an expert on American racial unrest. He was diagnosed with cancer in October 1973 and died at Thiais, near Paris, on 5 November 1974 (Wikipedia).
literary_profile: Four novels, Last of the Conquerors (Farrar, Straus, 1948), Anger at Innocence (1950), South Street (1954) and The Stone Face (1963), and the reportage Return to Black America (Prentice-Hall, 1970), with essays and journalism, among them 'The Negro Writer: Pitfalls and Compensations' (Phylon, 1950) (Wikipedia).
stylistic_characteristics: Realist protest fiction, which Kirkus found didactic and flat in prose but capable of 'fine oblique scenes' and shocking comparisons between ghettos, camps and riots; Wikipedia describes him using fiction, as he used journalism, to testify to events he witnessed.
intellectual_concerns: Racism in the United States and abroad, from the segregated army of occupation to the Algerian War; interracial love; exile and the outsider's double view of two countries; the choice between militancy and withdrawal.
historical_significance: Wikipedia links him with the Black social protest novel of Wright, Ellison, Motley and Petry and counts South Street among the first Black militant protest novels. Kristin Ross notes that The Stone Face, published in the United States because it could not be published in France, remained one of the few representations of the massacre of 17 October 1961 until the early 1990s; New York Review Books reissued it in 2021 with an introduction by Adam Shatz.
bibliographical_notes: Bibliography status, 1946-2000: substantially complete for books (Wikipedia's list of major works); journalism incomplete. Recorded: Last of the Conquerors (New York: Farrar, Straus, 1948; London: Gollancz, 1949); South Street (New York: Farrar, Straus and Young, 1954); The Stone Face (New York: Farrar, Straus, 1963; New York Review Books, 2021). Listed and not recorded, because no source consulted describes their contents: Anger at Innocence (Farrar, Straus, 1950; London: Gollancz, 1951; in French as Malheur aux justes, 1952) and Return to Black America (Englewood Cliffs: Prentice-Hall, 1970; in French as L'Amerique noire, 1972), reportage revised from his journalism of the late 1960s. Essays and articles include 'The Negro Writer: Pitfalls and Compensations' (Phylon, 1950) and 'Black Boy in France' (Ebony, July 1953), on Richard Wright in Paris.
